# Jean Baudrillard · Simulation — preliminary outline
Literature and Visual Media · Semester 3, Unit 1

## Reading limitation
The exact boundaries of the prescribed “Postmodern and Popular Culture Simulations” selection have not been independently confirmed. This is a conceptual introduction, not a complete summary of the assigned text. Check the course anthology before relying on specific examples or quotations.

## Representation and simulation
A common model of representation assumes an image refers back to an original reality, which it may represent accurately or distort. Baudrillard asks what happens when models, signs and mediated representations organise what a society experiences as real. Simulation is not simply lying: its force lies in complicating the distinction between a copy and an independently accessible original.

## Hyperreality and Disneyland
Hyperreality describes a condition in which models and signs can become more decisive than any stable original they seem to represent. Baudrillard’s discussion of Disneyland suggests that presenting the park as an imaginary space can make the world outside appear simply real, even though that outside world is also mediated and constructed. This is his provocative argument, not a factual claim that people or material conditions do not exist.

## Apply and question
Consider a carefully designed online profile. It selects images and styles that may influence how someone is perceived. This can illustrate mediation, but a curated profile alone does not prove Baudrillard’s larger claim about simulation. Ask what evidence would support or challenge the argument.

## Lesson and questions
0–10 min: distinguish a map from a landscape. 10–25: compare representation and simulation. 25–38: examine the Disneyland example. 38–45: discuss a digital example and its limits. 45–50: explain why simulation is not merely a synonym for “fake.”

# Raymond Williams · Culture, Art and Democracy
Literature and Visual Media · Semester 3

## A guide to Keywords
In Keywords, Raymond Williams investigates the historical and contested uses of important social words. A keyword is not simply a term with one correct, timeless meaning: changes in its uses can reveal social and political struggles. The following is an introduction; consult the exact entries and edition for their detailed histories.

## Culture
The word has histories associated with cultivation and development. Williams distinguishes, among other uses, intellectual or artistic development, a particular way of life, and works or practices of intellectual and artistic activity. These senses coexist and can conflict. Calling something culture may praise “high art,” describe a shared practice, or refer to a process of learning; context matters.

## Art
Art has been associated with skill and making as well as more specialised senses of creative and aesthetic practice. Its separation into a distinct category from craft and other skilled activity has a history. Ask who has the authority to designate a film, song or image as art and what kinds of labour may be overlooked.

## Democracy
Democracy concerns rule or power of the people, but “the people,” representation, participation and equality have been understood differently. Formal voting is one important dimension; democratic control and social equality are also contested questions. Williams’s historical approach prevents a single present-day definition from erasing conflict over the term.

## A classroom application
Compare the sentence “Cinema is art” with “Cinema is part of popular culture.” Do the two statements contradict each other? Identify the sense of each word and discuss how both can be true.

# Roland Barthes · The Photographic Message
Literature and Visual Media · Semester 3

## Central question
How can a photograph appear to show reality directly while also carrying meanings shaped by culture? Barthes examines the press photograph as part of a communicative setting that includes producers, publication, surrounding text and readers.

## Denotation and connotation
At a basic level a photograph seems to show what was in front of the camera: its denoted message. Barthes calls attention to the photograph’s apparent status as a message without a code, but he also analyses connotation: meanings produced through cultural assumptions and editorial choices. This coexistence is the “photographic paradox.” Do not conclude that a photograph has no relationship to what was photographed; ask how that relationship is framed and interpreted.

## How connotation is constructed
Barthes discusses procedures including trick effects, pose, objects, photogenia (such as lighting and technical treatment), aestheticism and syntax, or meaning produced by a sequence of images. A caption can direct interpretation, adding information or emphasis that is not self-evident in the photograph. A familiar gesture or object may signal different things to different audiences.

## Worked example
A picture shows a person holding a folder outside a building: that is a basic description. A low camera angle, official emblem and caption calling the person a “leader” can suggest authority. Another caption could emphasise a protest or controversy. Neither interpretation should be treated as self-evident without examining the broader context.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: describe an image without evaluating it. 10–22: distinguish denotation and connotation. 22–35: compare two captions for the same image. 35–45: identify one photographic procedure and its potential effect. 45–50: write an evidence-based interpretation.

## Questions

# Nicholas Mirzoeff · What is Visual Culture?
Literature and Visual Media · Semester 3

## Central idea
Mirzoeff introduces visual culture as a way of examining visual events: situations in which a person encounters visual information, meaning or pleasure through a technology or practice of seeing. His introduction draws attention to everyday visual experience, not only the gallery or cinema.

## Concepts
Visualisation makes an issue, process or place available to sight through an image, map, screen, chart or representation. It is a social and technological practice, not a transparent window onto every aspect of the world. Spectatorship asks how people look and how situations invite, guide or restrict looking. Visual literacy involves learning to question images and their contexts.

Mirzoeff’s attention to screens and visual technologies is influential. A critic might ask whether this emphasis overlooks other everyday visual experiences, including buildings, public space or bodies. The question is an invitation to debate the field’s scope, not proof that Mirzoeff denies the existence of those objects.

## Apply the idea
For a map on a phone, ask what is shown, what is left out, who designed its categories, what data supports it, and whose movement it makes easier. Compare this with looking at a family photograph: both are visual events, but they involve different purposes and relationships.

# Gender, race, religion and caste in visual media
Literature and Visual Media · Semester 3

## Representation and power
Gender is not simply a fixed set of roles that images mirror: ideas about femininity, masculinity and other gender identities are learned, negotiated and contested in social life. Media can repeat conventions, challenge them or do both. Ask who speaks, acts, watches, is watched and has authority. Avoid assuming that all viewers respond identically.

Race and ethnicity are historically constructed categories whose effects are real; visual stereotypes can naturalise inequality. Religion may appear through clothing, spaces, rituals or narrative roles, but no single image represents an entire faith. Caste is a specific historically embedded hierarchy in South Asia: do not treat it as interchangeable with race or class. Analyse representation together with material conditions, production, distribution and audience.

Globalisation moves images, media industries, genres and audiences across borders. It can expand access and collaboration, while unequal ownership and distribution can concentrate power. Local audiences also interpret and adapt imported forms; global influence is not simply passive imitation.

## Classroom practice
Select a short clip. Record camera position, dialogue, who has decision-making power and what the narrative expects viewers to know. Then ask whose point of view is absent and whether an apparently familiar image relies on stereotypes. Respect participants’ lived experiences; nobody must speak for an entire community.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: define representation and stereotype. 10–22: examine gender roles in a short example. 22–35: discuss race, religion and caste without equating them. 35–45: analyse circulation and globalisation. 45–50: cite a precise feature and offer an interpretation.

# Fanon and Dyer · race, looking and the norm
Literature and Visual Media · Semester 3

## Fanon: The Fact of Blackness
In a chapter of Black Skin, White Masks, translated under different titles including “The Fact of Blackness” and “The Lived Experience of the Black Man,” Frantz Fanon describes how a racist gaze imposes meanings on a Black person’s body. A child’s fearful recognition is not an innocent neutral observation: it draws upon a history of colonial stereotypes. Fanon’s discussion of a racialised bodily schema shows how racism can disrupt ordinary bodily experience and force a person to encounter themselves through another’s judgement.

Fanon’s chapter moves through anger, analysis, attempts at self-assertion and debates about history and Black identity. It is not simply a statement that looking itself is always oppressive, or that Black identity is reducible to what white observers think. Attend to the translation, the chapter’s changing voice and historical context.

## Dyer: White
Richard Dyer asks why whiteness in much Western visual culture can be treated as ordinary or universal while other groups are explicitly marked as racial. Making whiteness visible as a constructed racial position allows representation and power to be examined rather than taking a presumed norm for granted. Lighting, casting and narrative point of view are among possible objects of analysis. The course title may refer to an essay or extract: confirm the assigned selection.

## Compare
Fanon foregrounds the embodied effect of being made an object of a racialising look; Dyer examines how a dominant position can escape notice as a norm. They are related but not interchangeable. For a film still, ask whose perspective is centred and what evidence supports the claim.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: explain “unmarked norm.” 10–22: discuss Fanon’s account of the gaze. 22–35: examine Dyer’s question about whiteness. 35–45: compare their methods using an image. 45–50: write one similarity and one difference.

# Vittorio De Sica · Bicycle Thieves
Literature and Visual Media · Semester 3

## Film overview
Bicycle Thieves (1948) is set in postwar Rome. Antonio Ricci, who has been unemployed, obtains work putting up posters, but the job requires a bicycle. His wife Maria pawns the family’s sheets so he can recover his bicycle from the pawnshop.

## Story from beginning to end
On Antonio’s first day at work the bicycle is stolen. The police take a report but offer little immediate hope of recovery. Antonio and his young son Bruno search the city with help from acquaintances, visiting markets where bicycle parts are traded. They follow leads, but an old man associated with the suspect escapes their questioning.

The search strains the father–son relationship. Antonio strikes Bruno in frustration; later he fears his son may have drowned, only to find him safe. They eat together, and a glimpse of another family’s comfort sharpens the contrast between their circumstances and their hopes.

Antonio eventually confronts the suspected thief in his neighbourhood. The young man’s neighbours defend him, and the officer called to the scene cannot establish the accusation from the available evidence. Antonio leaves without the bicycle. Near a football stadium he sees many bicycles and attempts to steal an unattended one. The owner and others catch him. Bruno sees the humiliation; the owner decides not to press charges. Father and son walk away hand in hand in the crowd. Antonio’s bicycle is not recovered, and the film does not show a secure solution to his livelihood.

## Form and interpretation
Italian neorealism is associated with attention to ordinary people, locations and social conditions, though individual films differ. The bicycle is both a practical means of work and a focus for dignity and dependence. The ending complicates a simple distinction between victim and thief without making poverty an excuse that settles every ethical question.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: establish the employment problem. 10–25: map the search and the father–son relationship. 25–35: compare the first theft with Antonio’s attempted theft. 35–45: analyse the final crowd and handholding. 45–50: exit response with one precise scene.

## Questions
Why does one object matter so much? How does Bruno’s viewpoint affect the ending? What remains unresolved?

# Walter Salles · The Motorcycle Diaries
Literature and Visual Media · Semester 3

## Film overview
The Motorcycle Diaries (2004) dramatises a 1952 South American journey by young medical student Ernesto Guevara and his friend Alberto Granado. Based on travel accounts, the film is a retrospective narrative rather than a transparent record of every historical event.

## Journey and ending
Ernesto and Alberto leave Argentina on an ageing motorcycle, La Poderosa. Early mishaps and breakdowns give the journey an adventurous, comic quality. After the motorcycle can no longer carry them, they continue by other means. Encounters with workers, displaced people and Indigenous communities bring poverty and inequality more sharply into view. The film contrasts the travellers’ relative privilege with the experiences they witness.

In Peru they visit Machu Picchu and reflect on Indigenous histories and colonial power. At San Pablo they work with people affected by Hansen’s disease, then commonly called leprosy. The film represents separation between patients and staff and shows Ernesto resisting stigma. On his birthday he speaks of a more united Latin America and swims across the river to the patients’ side, despite his asthma. The crossing is a dramatic image of solidarity; it should not be mistaken for a medical recommendation. Hansen’s disease is treatable, and film depictions should not be used as medical advice.

The travellers leave and later part in Venezuela. The ending places the youthful journey beside the men’s later histories. The film suggests political awakening, but the journey alone does not explain every aspect of Guevara’s subsequent politics or establish a simple historical cause.

## Film form and questions
How does the road-movie structure change from adventure to social observation? Whose experiences are seen through the travellers’ eyes? How does the river acquire symbolic meaning? Compare a film scene with a historical source without assuming either is neutral.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: introduce a road film and biographical adaptation. 10–25: trace three encounters. 25–35: examine framing of illness and stigma. 35–45: analyse the river crossing. 45–50: distinguish a filmic choice from a historical claim.

# Film theory · seven approaches and key terms
Literature and Visual Media · Semester 3

## Before interpreting: film language
A shot is an uninterrupted recorded or edited view; a scene generally gathers action in a place and time. Framing selects what appears within the image. Mise-en-scène includes the arrangement of setting, costume, lighting, bodies and movement. Editing connects shots; sound may come from the represented world (diegetic) or be added for the audience (nondiegetic). These terms are tools for noticing evidence, not automatic interpretations.

## Seven approaches
Auteur approaches study patterns associated with a director, while recognising that cinema is collaborative and shaped by producers, performers, technicians and institutions. Gender film theory asks how films construct gender, looking and spectatorship; different feminist and queer critics do not all make the same argument.

Formalism examines how composition, editing, sound and performance make effects; it does not require ignoring history. Marxist approaches connect cultural form to class, labour, ownership and ideology, but differ in their accounts of economic power. Psychoanalytic approaches use theories of desire, identification and the unconscious to interpret spectatorship or narrative; they are theoretical frameworks, not clinical diagnoses of audiences.

Structuralism asks how meaning emerges from relations, contrasts and conventions rather than isolated elements. Genre studies examines recurring conventions and variation in industrial, historical and audience contexts. A film may cross genres.

## Worked comparison
A sequence of a worker in a factory might be analysed for rapid cuts (formalist), labour relations (Marxist), gendered division of work (gender theory), or its relation to the director’s other films (auteur). Strong analysis explains how the chosen evidence supports a claim rather than attaching labels.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: identify shot, framing and sound. 10–25: introduce four approaches with examples. 25–35: compare the remaining approaches. 35–45: groups analyse one scene using two lenses. 45–50: exit ticket explaining how interpretations differ.

# Bazin and Harman · realism, editing and signs
Literature and Visual Media · Semester 3

## André Bazin: The Evolution of the Language of Cinema
Bazin discusses different directions in film history, contrasting filmmakers who emphasise the constructed image and montage with those who place greater faith in the revelation of reality. Montage can produce meanings through the relation between shots; it is not merely the fact that a film has cuts. Bazin considers deep focus and staging in depth important because multiple elements can remain visible within a shot, offering the spectator choices about where to look and preserving a degree of ambiguity.

Do not state that Bazin thought any edited film was false or that a long take is automatically neutral. Framing and staging also guide attention. Ask what evidence a particular scene supplies and whether a viewer truly has unrestricted choice.

## Gilbert Harman: Semiotics and the Cinema: Metz and Wollen
Semiotics studies signs and meaning. Christian Metz explores cinema as a signifying practice; Peter Wollen develops another account drawing on approaches to signs. Harman examines and questions assumptions in these theories, including how “code” is used. Do not treat his essay as a simple endorsement of a single film grammar or claim that every shot functions like a word in spoken language.

## Worked comparison
A cut from a face to a closed door may prompt an inference about what a character sees or fears. A longer shot showing the character and door together still selects a position and duration. Compare the kinds of information available in each version, then ask how a viewer learns the conventions needed to understand them.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: review shot and edit. 10–22: explain Bazin on depth and ambiguity. 22–35: discuss sign and code with a film example. 35–45: debate advantages and limits of each framework. 45–50: exit ticket contrasting montage and deep-focus staging.

# Charlie Chaplin · City Lights
Literature and Visual Media · Semester 3

## Introduction
City Lights (1931), a largely silent romantic comedy with synchronised music and effects, follows Chaplin’s Tramp in a city divided by wealth. The film includes a suicide attempt; introduce the subject sensitively.

## Story overview
The Tramp meets a blind flower seller and buys a flower. A sequence involving a car door leads her to mistake him for a wealthy man. He becomes fond of her. That night he encounters a drunken millionaire attempting suicide and helps him; the millionaire treats him warmly while intoxicated but fails to recognise him when sober. Their recurring encounters produce comedy as the Tramp moves between luxury and exclusion.

The flower seller and her grandmother face money problems. The Tramp takes work and tries to obtain enough money for rent and a proposed operation. His comic attempt to win a boxing prize fails. The intoxicated millionaire later gives him money, but burglars rob the millionaire and knock him unconscious. The police find the Tramp with the money, and the millionaire cannot remember giving it to him. The Tramp gets the money to the flower seller and is arrested.

After a period in prison, he returns to the street and finds that the woman’s sight has been restored and she now works in a flower shop. She does not initially recognise him and offers the poorly dressed man a flower and a coin. Touching his hand, she recognises her benefactor. Their final exchange and expressions invite tenderness and uncertainty; the film does not show their later life together.

## Form and questions
Pantomime, timing, composition and recurring misunderstandings carry much of the story. Compare the millionaire’s drunken and sober treatment of the Tramp. How do class and appearance affect recognition? Discuss disability respectfully: the film’s use of blindness is a narrative convention, not a general truth about blind people.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: silent-film and sound context. 10–25: map recognition and mistaken identity. 25–35: examine a gesture in the final scene. 35–45: discuss class and the film’s representation of disability. 45–50: exit ticket on how performance conveys meaning.

# Sergei Eisenstein · Battleship Potemkin
Literature and Visual Media · Semester 3

## Context
Eisenstein’s 1925 silent Soviet film reworks the 1905 mutiny on the battleship Potemkin. It is a political film as well as a landmark in editing. Its images of violence require a content warning. The film is a constructed interpretation, not a documentary record of every incident shown.

## Five-part story
1. Sailors are ordered to eat meat they believe is rotten. Their complaints reveal the officers’ contempt and the unequal conditions aboard ship.
2. The confrontation escalates into a mutiny when sailors refuse to submit to punishment. The ship is taken from the officers; the sailor Vakulinchuk is mortally wounded.
3. At Odesa, his body becomes a focus of public mourning. People gather, and solidarity between townspeople and sailors grows.
4. In the famous Odessa Steps sequence, troops move against civilians. Rapidly connected images of running crowds, soldiers and injured people create fear and collective outrage. A baby carriage descending the steps becomes a memorable image within the sequence. The sequence should not be presented as a literal filmed record of a specific massacre on those exact steps.
5. A squadron approaches the Potemkin. Rather than destroy the rebellious ship, the sailors allow it to pass. The film concludes with an image of solidarity.

## Montage and ideology
Montage creates relationships across shots. In the steps sequence, editing combines movement, repeated angles and fragmented bodies to intensify the event and organise an emotional and political response. Compare this with Bazin’s interest in ambiguity and staging in depth, without assuming either filmmaker uses only one technique.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: distinguish 1905 event and 1925 representation. 10–22: outline five parts. 22–35: examine a short, appropriately chosen montage sequence. 35–45: discuss how editing produces an interpretation. 45–50: exit ticket connecting two shots to an effect.

## Questions
Why does the film use collective crowds? How does editing reshape time? What are the ethical responsibilities of interpreting a violent historical representation?

# Genre, narrative and criticism across media
Literature and Visual Media · Semester 3

## Film and narrative
A story is a sequence of events as understood by a reader or viewer; narration is how a work presents information, including order, viewpoint and omission. Film and fiction can both use a restricted perspective or a flashback, but film also works through moving images, sound, performance and editing. Avoid assuming that a film’s camera is always equivalent to a novel’s narrator.

Theatre and film share performance, space and time, but editing and camera position can create relations not available in the same way in a live performance. Theatre also has distinctive possibilities of shared space and live presence. Films interact with music, painting, photography and other arts.

## Genre and alternative forms
Genres are historically changing groupings of conventions, institutions and expectations; a film can mix them. Film noir is often associated with crime, shadowed imagery and moral uncertainty, but scholars debate whether it is a genre, style or cycle. Documentary makes claims about the world through selected images and sounds; it is constructed even when addressing real events. Queer and subaltern cinema are not single styles: consider whose experiences, authorship and structures of power are involved.

## Prescribed critical readings
Stephen Neale’s “Film Noir” should be read for its specific argument about classification and history rather than reduced to a checklist. S. Theodore Baskaran’s “Patriotic Cinema: An Aspect of the Freedom Struggle” asks for attention to the historical relation of cinema and anticolonial politics; verify the assigned essay’s examples in the original. In “Reading Against the Reel,” Sundar Sarukkai argues that criticism connects a film, a reviewer’s standpoint and audiences, helping a film have an afterlife in writing. Criticism need not be merely a recommendation to watch or avoid.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: define story and narration. 10–20: compare a written and filmed scene. 20–30: debate noir as a category. 30–40: consider documentary and political context. 40–50: write a short review based on one observed detail.

## Questions
How does a review illuminate rather than simply rate? Why does a historical context matter to an account of patriotic cinema?

## Stephen Neale: Film Noir
Film noir is often associated with crime, hard-edged or uncertain morality and distinctive lighting, but the category is contested. Neale’s genre scholarship encourages attention to how genres are defined historically, including industrial and critical uses, rather than assuming all examples share one timeless essence. Ask whether “noir” describes a genre recognised by producers at the time, a retrospective critical label, a style or a cycle. These positions need not be reduced to a single checklist.

# Akira Kurosawa · Rashomon
Literature and Visual Media · Semester 3

## Context and content note
Rashomon (1950) uses competing accounts of a violent encounter involving a samurai, his wife and a bandit. It includes sexual violence. Discuss the woman’s representation with care and do not treat the bandit’s version of consent as automatically reliable.

## Story and conflicting accounts
A woodcutter and a priest shelter from heavy rain at the ruined Rashomon gate. A commoner joins them. They discuss a case: a samurai has been found dead in a grove and the bandit Tajomaru has been captured. Testimonies are presented through the frame of their conversation.

Tajomaru says he lured and tied up the samurai, encountered the wife and killed her husband in a duel. His self-dramatising account presents him as bold. The wife describes the bandit’s assault and her husband’s contempt; in distress she faints and finds him dead. Through a medium, the dead samurai gives a different version, claiming that he killed himself after the encounter. Their accounts conflict about motives, actions and the death.

The woodcutter, who had originally said he found the body, offers another account after indicating that he witnessed the event. His version portrays a less heroic, awkward fight. The commoner questions his reliability and suggests that he may have taken the missing valuable dagger. The film does not supply a final, independently verified solution that makes one whole account certainly true.

A baby is found abandoned at the gate. The commoner takes its belongings and departs. The woodcutter offers to care for the child, and the priest’s damaged faith in people is tentatively renewed. The ending places an act of care beside unresolved deception.

## Form and questions
The film’s flashbacks do not simply replay an objectively known event: each account frames the past. Ask how gesture, camera, performance and editing shape the competing narratives. Does the ending answer the murder mystery, or offer a different kind of ethical response?

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: content note and framing situation. 10–25: chart four accounts without choosing a winner. 25–35: analyse credibility and motive. 35–45: discuss the child and the ending. 45–50: write one supported interpretation of uncertainty.

# Robert Bresson · Pickpocket
Literature and Visual Media · Semester 3

## Story
In Pickpocket (1959), Michel, an isolated young man in Paris, steals from a woman at a racetrack. He is arrested but released for lack of evidence. His mother is ill, and Jeanne, a neighbour who helps care for her, urges him to visit. His friend Jacques also tries to help him. Michel nevertheless grows increasingly absorbed in theft.

He practises and learns techniques from an experienced pickpocket. Sequences in stations and other crowded places concentrate on hands, wallets and coordinated movement. Michel discusses an idea that exceptional people might be entitled to break ordinary laws, but the film does not simply endorse his self-justification. His mother dies, and Michel continues to evade both the police inspector’s attention and close human relationships.

When he realises the police are watching, Michel leaves France. After a period away he returns and learns that Jeanne has a child and is struggling. He tries legitimate work but returns to theft. At the racetrack he steals from a man who is part of a police operation and is arrested. Jeanne visits him in prison. Their encounter across the bars suggests a movement towards connection or grace, but viewers may debate how complete that change is.

## Film form
Bresson’s restrained performances, ellipses, attention to hands and economical use of sound make viewers assemble motivations and actions. The film is related by critics to questions of crime and redemption, including comparisons with Dostoevsky; it is not a direct scene-by-scene adaptation of Crime and Punishment.

## Lesson: 50 minutes
0–10: contrast a crime plot with a character study. 10–25: trace Michel’s choices. 25–35: analyse a sequence of hands and objects. 35–45: discuss the prison ending. 45–50: write a claim supported by a filmic detail.

## Questions
What does Michel’s theory of exceptional people do for him? How does the focus on hands shape our understanding? What different meanings might Jeanne’s visit have?

# Jean-Luc Godard · Breathless
Literature and Visual Media · Semester 3

## Story
In Breathless (1960), small-time criminal Michel Poiccard steals a car and kills a police officer during a pursuit. He reaches Paris and reconnects with Patricia, an American student and aspiring journalist selling newspapers. He tries to obtain money and persuade her to leave with him for Italy, while the police search for him.

Their time together includes extended conversations about love, freedom, identity and their uncertain relationship. Patricia is attracted to Michel but also questions what she feels and what his criminal situation means. The police contact her. Eventually she informs them of Michel’s whereabouts and tells him what she has done. Michel does not initially flee. When the police arrive he is shot and collapses in the street. His final words are difficult for Patricia to understand and vary in translation; she repeats a gesture associated with him and addresses a question about the word used. The film does not make her motives or the meaning of the final exchange completely transparent.

## Technique and context
The film is associated with the French New Wave. Jump cuts can interrupt apparent continuity within a scene, making editing noticeable. Location shooting, references to cinema and a loose crime narrative combine familiarity with disruption. Michel’s imitation of American gangster style is an example of intertextuality: another film tradition becomes part of his self-presentation.

## Teaching questions
How does the film use and unsettle crime-film expectations? What do the jump cuts do to time and movement? How do Michel and Patricia imagine freedom differently? How might different subtitles affect interpretation of the final scene?

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: introduce the French New Wave. 10–22: outline the pursuit and relationship. 22–35: examine editing and cinema references. 35–45: discuss Patricia’s decision without assuming a single motive. 45–50: exit ticket on form and effect.

# Reading film as text · form, discourse and ideology
Literature and Visual Media · Semester 3

## What does “film as text” mean?
A film can be treated as an organised object of interpretation, not because it is literally a written page, but because images, sounds, performances and narrative relations can be analysed. An interpretation begins with precise description: identify a scene, what is visible and audible, the sequence of shots and relevant context.

## Discourse and ideology
A discourse is a way of organising language, images and assumptions around a subject. Ask how a film makes some statements or identities appear obvious and others difficult to express. Ideology refers to patterns of ideas and practices connected with power; a film can negotiate conflicting positions rather than expressing one simple message. Analysis needs evidence from form and context, not just a label.

## Step-by-step method
1. Describe a specific moment: who is present, what happens and what is heard?
2. Identify a formal choice: framing, duration, camera angle, lighting, editing, sound or performance.
3. Explain a possible effect: what does the choice invite a viewer to notice or feel?
4. Connect it to representation or power while recognising alternative readings.
5. Check the film’s historical and production context. A claim about an audience’s actual response needs audience evidence; it cannot be proven from the shot alone.

## Example
A character framed alone in a crowded station might suggest isolation. That is an interpretation supported by composition, not proof of what every viewer feels. Compare the scene’s sound and neighbouring shots before deciding whether the interpretation holds.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: distinguish description and interpretation. 10–20: define discourse and ideology. 20–35: analyse a brief film scene in pairs. 35–45: compare two interpretations and their evidence. 45–50: exit ticket on one formal feature and a supported effect.

# Ray, Pandian and Prasad · studying Indian cinema
Literature and Visual Media · Semester 3

## Satyajit Ray: What Is Wrong with Indian Films?
In this historically situated critical essay, Ray argues that filmmaking needs imagination, planning and sensitivity to the medium rather than a reliance on imitation or technical gloss. He criticises aspects of contemporary production and calls for films grounded in the contexts they represent. Treat this as Ray’s argument from a particular historical moment, not a timeless verdict on all Indian films. Ask whether his ideas of realism and national style exclude other valuable forms, including popular song-and-dance cinema.

## M. S. S. Pandian: Tamil Cultural Elites and Cinema
Pandian’s essay examines relations between Tamil cultural elites and cinema. A productive starting question is how judgements about taste, respectability, popular entertainment and realism can be connected to caste and class. Do not assume that “elite” describes every person or that one attitude exhausts Tamil film history. Read the article for its historical examples and specific argument before attributing a detailed claim to it.

## M. Madhava Prasad: Ideology of the Hindi Film
Prasad’s study connects cinematic forms to political and economic history. One important concept, “feudal family romance,” helps analyse how certain narratives organise authority through family and social hierarchy, even as they also include modern desires and institutions. It is an analytical category for particular films and historical conditions, not a claim that all Hindi films have one plot. A scholarly review linked below also questions aspects of the historical fit; engage with disagreement rather than treating a framework as a formula.

## Compare and discuss
How does Ray’s judgement of style differ from Pandian’s analysis of cultural authority? How might Prasad connect a family ending to a wider structure of power? Use a scene and the assigned reading to substantiate the comparison.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: define historical context. 10–22: identify Ray’s claim. 22–32: discuss who gets to define good taste. 32–42: apply a family-authority question to a film scene. 42–50: exit ticket distinguishing an author’s argument from your own.

# Satyajit Ray · Pather Panchali
Literature and Visual Media · Semester 3

## Introduction
Pather Panchali (1955) is Satyajit Ray’s Bengali film adapted from Bibhutibhushan Bandyopadhyay’s novel. The film follows a family in rural Bengal through everyday pleasures, poverty and bereavement. This note describes the film, not every event of the novel.

## Story from beginning to end
Harihar Ray, a priest and aspiring writer, struggles to support his family. His wife Sarbajaya manages the household and cares for their daughter Durga; an elderly relative, Indir Thakrun, also lives with them at times. Sarbajaya’s frustration with scarce resources contributes to conflict with Indir, while Durga shares affection and small treats with her.

Apu is born and grows up close to his older sister. The children explore their surroundings, watch travelling entertainers and follow a sweet seller they cannot afford. In a celebrated sequence they move through fields and discover a passing train. Their curiosity and delight coexist with the family’s economic difficulties. Indir leaves after conflict and dies away from the house; the children encounter her body.

Harihar travels in search of work, leaving Sarbajaya to manage an increasingly difficult situation. Durga is accused of stealing a neighbour’s necklace. During the monsoon the children enjoy the rain, but Durga falls ill and dies during a violent storm while her father is away. Do not infer a particular medical diagnosis from a short plot summary.

Harihar returns with gifts, not knowing of the death. When he shows the sari he has bought for Durga, Sarbajaya breaks down and he learns what has happened. As the family prepares to leave, Apu discovers the necklace hidden among Durga’s belongings and throws it into a pond. Harihar, Sarbajaya and Apu depart their village by cart for a new life. The film’s ending does not show the events of the later Apu films.

## Form and interpretation
Attention to landscape, sound, faces, everyday action and changes in pace gives small events weight. The train can be read as an image of discovery and a wider changing world; support an interpretation with the scene rather than treating a single symbolism as compulsory. Sarbajaya’s harshness and tenderness should be considered alongside the pressures she faces.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: introduce family and adaptation. 10–25: map the children’s experiences and the family’s pressures. 25–35: discuss one use of sound or landscape. 35–45: analyse the homecoming and departure. 45–50: exit response on a detail and its effect.

## Questions
How does the film combine play with hardship? What changes when Harihar returns? Why might Apu throw the necklace away?

## Before class
Read the prescribed essay or view the assigned film in the department’s edition. These notes are teaching aids, not replacements for the work; interpretations should be tested against specific passages or shots.

# Anand Patwardhan · Jai Bhim Comrade
Literature and Visual Media · Semester 3

## Introduction and content note
Jai Bhim Comrade (2011) is a documentary by Anand Patwardhan made over many years. It addresses caste discrimination, police violence and the politics of Dalit cultural expression. The film includes accounts of deaths and suicide; offer a content note and allow sensitive discussion.

## Structure and major subjects
The documentary takes the 1997 police firing in Mumbai’s Ramabai Ambedkar Nagar as a starting point. Residents had protested the desecration of a statue of B. R. Ambedkar; police opened fire, killing people. The film connects this event with the death of Dalit poet and singer Vilas Ghogre, who died by suicide after the violence.

Rather than following a single fictional plot, the film moves among testimony, songs, archival materials, political gatherings and arguments about caste, labour and collective action. It attends to Ambedkar’s legacy and to tensions and alliances in Dalit and left politics. Interviews and songs allow speakers to articulate experiences and positions, while selection, editing and the filmmaker’s perspective shape how audiences encounter them. The documentary’s construction does not by itself make the events imaginary or the testimony unimportant.

## Key approaches
Ask who is speaking, what knowledge they claim, how the film positions their testimony, and how a song differs from an interview in its emotional and political work. Avoid presenting Dalit communities as passive objects: the film records organised protest and cultural production. Historical claims about the police firing and legal proceedings should be checked against reliable reporting as well as the film.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: establish respectful discussion and historical context. 10–22: outline the event and the documentary’s scope. 22–35: analyse an interview or song in a suitable excerpt. 35–45: discuss editing, evidence and filmmaker position. 45–50: exit ticket distinguishing a documented event from an interpretation.

## Questions
What can song communicate that an interview may not? How can a documentary be constructed and still investigate real events? How does the film relate caste to political organising?

Read the prescribed essay or view the assigned film in the department’s edition. These notes are teaching aids, not replacements for the work; interpretations should be tested against specific passages or shots.

# Content writing · purpose, audience and process
Content Writing · Semester 3, Unit 1

## What is content writing?
Content writing creates written material for a defined audience and purpose: to explain, inform, help a reader complete a task, build a relationship or support an action. Forms include web pages, articles, newsletters, reports, case studies and product information. Not every piece is an advertisement. A good content writer works with subject specialists, editors, designers and publishers, and checks that claims are supported.

## Role and responsibilities
A writer interprets a brief, researches, identifies the audience’s questions, structures information, drafts, edits and adapts the work to its medium. Responsibilities include accuracy, accessible language, respectful representation, source acknowledgement, deadlines and adherence to the organisation’s style guide. An editor or subject expert may review specialist claims; a writer should not invent credentials or first-hand experience.

## Print and web
A print reader may encounter a continuous page sequence; a web reader may arrive directly at one section from a search or link. Online headings, informative link text and mobile-friendly paragraphs help navigation. Print also needs clear structure. Neither medium requires a fixed sentence length or arbitrary word count. Search engine optimisation (SEO) can make useful content easier to discover, but repeated keywords and empty claims do not substitute for helping the reader.

## The content process
1. Brief: define audience, topic, desired outcome, format, deadline, evidence and approval process.
2. Research: use reliable sources, note publication dates and record links or references.
3. Structure: arrange the answer in a useful order and identify gaps.
4. Draft: use clear headings, examples and a consistent voice.
5. Review: verify claims, links, accessibility, rights and style.
6. Publish and maintain: correct errors and revisit information when circumstances change.

## Worked example
Brief: “Help first-year students find library books.” Audience: new students. Outcome: find a book and know whom to ask. Outline: catalogue search, understanding availability, finding the shelf, requesting help. Do not invent the library’s hours or rules; verify them locally.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: compare information and persuasion. 10–20: identify audience and purpose in a brief. 20–30: draft a practical outline. 30–42: write the opening and one section. 42–50: peer-check usefulness and identify two facts requiring verification.

## Check yourself
What distinguishes audience from purpose? How does a web heading help a reader? Why is publishing not the end of the process?

course-18:1.text:
# Content formats · research, drafting and editing
Content Writing · Semester 3, Unit 2

## From brief to draft
Clarify the reader, objective, length, medium, deadline and constraints. Generate ideas, then research before choosing the strongest supported ones. Organise a logical outline and write a draft. Check the style sheet for spelling, punctuation, capitalisation, terminology, tone and citation conventions. Edit structure and flow before proofreading individual errors.

## Formats and purposes
An essay develops an idea or argument with explanations and evidence. A report presents information or findings for a defined purpose, often with sections and recommendations. Newspaper writing gives readers relevant verified information, distinguishes reporting from opinion and answers important questions clearly. Advertising aims to persuade and should not disguise unsupported claims as facts.

A blog can explain, reflect, report or advise; a useful post has a clear topic, helpful headings and sources where appropriate. A case study describes a particular situation, the action taken and the results, supported by evidence and permission; do not invent customer outcomes. A white paper explores a complex issue or proposed solution in detail and should distinguish evidence from a company’s promotional interest.

## Corporate writing
B2B addresses organisations; a reader may need compatibility, procurement and implementation details. B2C addresses individual consumers; a reader may need price, availability and practical benefits. Neither audience is uniform. A press release gives newsworthy, verifiable information with an attributable contact and date; it is not a guarantee of media coverage. A newsletter selects useful updates for subscribers and makes any promotional purpose clear.

## Tone, jargon and market research
Choose a formal or informal register for the reader and context. Explain necessary specialist terms; avoid jargon used only to sound impressive. Market research can include interviews, surveys and analysis of common questions, but respect consent and privacy. Separate verified findings from assumptions about the audience.

## Example: one fact in two formats
Verified event information: a library workshop is on Friday at 4 p.m. A news brief reports the event and source. An invitation might say, “Join the library workshop on Friday at 4 p.m.” Neither version should invent a venue, registration link or promised outcome.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: unpack a brief. 10–20: compare blog, report and press release. 20–32: outline a case study without fabricating results. 32–42: revise for audience and style sheet. 42–50: exchange proofreading checklists and write one evidence question.

## Questions
How does a case study differ from a white paper? Why can a B2B reader still need plain language? What should be checked before a press release is sent?

course-18:2.text:
# Visual and interactive content
Content Writing · Semester 3, Unit 3

## Visual content
An infographic combines visual organisation with information to make relationships or processes easier to understand. Begin with a clear point and reliable data; label units, dates and sources. Avoid misleading scales, distorted comparisons and visual decoration that obscures the message. An accompanying text summary or data table makes complex information available to readers who cannot use the graphic.

Images and screenshots can illustrate a product, step or situation. Choose images relevant to the message; obtain appropriate permission or a suitable licence. Check screenshots for private information, old interfaces and unreadably small text. Alternative text should convey an informative image’s purpose in context; decorative images can use an empty alternative. A complex chart needs more than a short alt text: supply its information in nearby text or a table.

## Video, memes and demonstrations
A product demonstration shows a real task in a sequence: introduce the goal, show the steps, explain limitations and give the next action. Use accurate captions for meaningful audio and provide a transcript; describe important visual information as needed. Memes and GIFs draw on shared conventions and can create humour, but context, copyright, access and potential offence matter. Avoid essential information conveyed only through a moving image.

The syllabus extract says “30-degree videos.” This may be a formatting or source error; check the original syllabus and teacher’s instruction before assuming it means 360-degree video. If 360-degree video is intended, the viewer can explore a recorded environment; offer an accessible alternative and consider motion sensitivity.

## Interactive content
A quiz asks questions and provides feedback; a poll collects responses; an interactive white paper lets readers navigate or explore information. State purpose, explain how responses will be used, avoid collecting unnecessary personal data and test keyboard and screen-reader access. A poll is not automatically representative research: describe who responded and how they were selected.

## Free and paid tools
Choose tools by task, accessibility, data protection, export format, collaboration, licensing and total cost—not just the “free” label. Free tiers, limits and prices change. Do not upload confidential material to an external service without permission.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: compare a graphic and its text equivalent. 10–22: sketch an accessible infographic with a source. 22–32: draft a short demonstration script. 32–42: design a poll and identify sampling limitations. 42–50: peer-check rights, accessibility and privacy.

## Questions
What makes a visual misleading? Why do captions and text equivalents matter? What can a voluntary poll legitimately tell us?

course-18:3.text:
# Social media, public relations and originality
Content Writing · Semester 3, Unit 4

## Social media writing
A social-media post should fit its audience, platform and purpose while remaining understandable outside its original context. State the main message clearly, use accessible wording and link to a reliable source when a claim needs support. A platform may truncate text or display it differently on a phone, so place essential information where readers can find it. Check images, captions and contrast.

## Public relations
Public relations concerns communication and relationships between an organisation and its publics, including staff, customers, communities and journalists. A PR statement should identify the organisation, explain what is known and what action is being taken, and avoid claiming certainty where facts are still being checked. PR, advertising and independent journalism have different roles even when all use similar channels.

Example: “The library is closed today because of a power issue. We will share an update by 2 p.m.” is useful only if those details have been verified and someone will deliver the update. If the reopening time is unknown, say so rather than inventing one.

## Plagiarism and copyright are not identical
Plagiarism is presenting another’s words, ideas or work as one’s own under the relevant academic or professional rules. Copyright is a legal system governing certain uses of protected works; legal outcomes depend on jurisdiction, rights, licences and exceptions. Attribution alone does not necessarily grant permission to reuse a copyrighted image or text. Conversely, use may be lawful in a situation while still requiring attribution under a professional or institutional policy. Do not treat these notes as legal advice.

## Writing original copy
Record sources while researching. Put copied wording in quotation marks in notes, then draft your own structure and wording. Attribute ideas and quotations, verify permissions and licences, and check any AI-assisted text for accuracy, originality and rights issues. A similarity score is a prompt for review, not proof by itself of plagiarism or innocence.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: analyse an organisation’s audience and purpose. 10–22: write a clear service update. 22–35: distinguish quotation, paraphrase and copied text. 35–45: discuss attribution versus permission using an image example. 45–50: exit ticket naming one check before publication.

## Questions
Why should a crisis message identify uncertainty? Does crediting an image always give permission to use it? What makes a paraphrase genuinely independent?

# Copywriting for print, email, social media and websites
Content Writing · Semester 3, Unit 5

## Copywriting and audience
Copywriting uses words to support a specific response, such as learning about an event, comparing a product or signing up for a service. It may be persuasive, but should be accurate and clear. Before writing, identify the reader, their problem, the offer, supporting evidence, medium and desired action. A call to action (CTA) tells the reader what to do next; it should match a real destination or process.

## Build and edit a message
A practical sequence is audience need → relevant benefit → evidence → next step. A feature is what something does; a benefit is why that feature may matter to a particular reader. Example: “The reading room has adjustable lamps” is a feature; “Adjust the light for comfortable reading” is a possible benefit. Do not claim every person will find it comfortable, or imply a feature exists without verification.

## Adapt by medium
Print advertising must communicate the offer, necessary conditions and action in the space available. Email marketing needs a meaningful subject line, a relevant message, a clear action and compliance with applicable consent and unsubscribe requirements. Social copy may be brief, but should not omit important qualifications. Website content should help readers understand the offer and complete a task; headings and descriptive links support navigation. Avoid fake urgency, invented testimonials, hidden fees and claims that cannot be substantiated.

## Sample adaptation
For a verified free library orientation: print headline: “Find your way around the library.” Email subject: “Library orientation: Friday at 4 p.m.” Website button: “See orientation details.” Confirm the time, location and link before publication; these examples do not imply a real event.

## Editing checklist
Does the first line address the reader? Is the main claim accurate and supported? Are terms and conditions visible? Is the CTA specific and functional? Can the text be read on mobile? Has a second person checked names, numbers, punctuation and links?

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: distinguish features and benefits. 10–20: write an audience brief. 20–32: draft print and email versions of one offer. 32–42: rewrite for a website and social post. 42–50: peer review for clarity, evidence and ethical claims.

## Questions
Why is “everyone needs this” a weak audience definition? What makes a CTA misleading? How can a writer persuade without exaggeration?

# O. Henry · After Twenty Years
Functional English II · Semester 3

## Story overview
A police officer patrols a quiet New York street at night. A man waits in the doorway of a shop and explains that twenty years earlier, he and his friend Jimmy Wells agreed to meet at this spot at ten o’clock. The restaurant where they parted is gone, but the man has travelled from the West to keep the appointment. When he lights his cigar, the match briefly illuminates his face and a scar. He tells the officer about his friendship and apparent success. The officer leaves.

A little later another man approaches and calls him Bob. Bob believes he is Jimmy. They walk together, but in the brighter light of a shop window Bob notices that his companion’s nose is different and realises that he is not his friend. The stranger is a plainclothes officer, who arrests Bob as a man wanted in Chicago. He hands Bob a note from Jimmy.

The note reveals that the first officer was Jimmy: he had recognised Bob’s wanted face when the match was struck. Jimmy could not bring himself to make the arrest personally, so he obtained another officer to do it. Bob’s hand begins steady as he reads but trembles by the end. The story does not show a long reunion or tell us the outcome of the case.

## Analysis
The surprise ending depends on limited information and the reader’s assumptions about the first officer. The promise reveals loyalty even as the arrest creates a conflict between friendship and duty. The match and shop light enable two different recognitions. Bob’s material success should not be taken at face value as proof of honest achievement.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: predict what an appointment after twenty years might reveal. 10–25: sequence the meeting, recognition and arrest. 25–35: identify clues before the ending. 35–45: discuss Jimmy’s choice. 45–50: exit ticket on the role of light.

## Questions
Who first recognises whom? Why does Jimmy ask another officer to act? How does the note change our understanding of the earlier conversation?

# Mina Assadi · A Ring to Me is Bondage
Functional English II · Semester 3

## Poem summary
The speaker repeatedly gives unexpected meanings to familiar things. Rather than focusing on a prayer mat, she imagines many roads through gardens and describes prayer in relation to happiness, movement and birdsong. She questions conventional assumptions about place and attachment, naming solitude happiness, a desert home and what makes her sad love.

She imagines a person who plucks a flower as unable to see its value, and a net separating fish from water as destructive. Looking at the sea, she imagines a relation between smallness and vastness that changes when the sea joins the ocean. Later she describes memory, a cage and an unused thought through surprising equivalences. The ring becomes an image of bondage, and the poem returns to the opening roads and gardens.

## Interpretation and form
The ring can suggest restrictive possession or a conventional relationship, but the poem does not require every ring or every relationship to have one meaning. Its repeated “to me” phrasing foregrounds a particular speaker’s perspective. Paradox and unconventional definitions invite readers to question customary associations; the return to the roads gives the poem a circular shape. Nature, freedom and confinement are productive themes, not a reason to treat the speaker as opposed to all religion or community.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: students suggest associations for “ring” and “road.” 10–25: follow the speaker’s changed definitions. 25–35: discuss the net and cage images. 35–45: compare opening and ending. 45–50: write a supported interpretation of one paradox.

## Questions
Why does the poem use personal definitions? How do the roads and the ring contrast? Can the poem value freedom while also expressing sadness?

# Jamaica Kincaid · Girl
Functional English II · Semester 3

## Form and overview
“Girl” is a very short work built largely as a sequence of instructions, commonly read as a mother speaking to a daughter. Its domestic and linguistic details evoke a Caribbean setting. The narrative is not organised like a conventional plot with several scenes; the pressure of repeated commands is itself central to its effect.

## What happens
The dominant speaker tells the girl how and when to wash clothes, how to cook, sew, garden, behave in public and manage relationships. Practical knowledge is interwoven with warnings about reputation and sexuality. She tells the girl not to sing benna in Sunday school; the girl briefly protests that she does not do so. The main voice continues, often assuming that the girl is at risk of becoming sexually disreputable.

Near the end the speaker advises the girl to test bread for freshness. The girl asks what to do if the baker refuses to let her touch it. The speaker responds by questioning whether the girl will become the sort of woman the baker would not trust near the bread. The work ends there; it does not tell us what the girl later chooses or becomes.

## Themes and method
The speaker transmits useful knowledge while enforcing restrictive expectations. The rapid, semicolon-linked instructions can feel both protective and overwhelming. The daughter’s two brief responses make unequal speaking power audible. Avoid reducing the mother to a villain or assuming that care cancels the harm of shaming; both can operate together. The story’s particular Caribbean details matter alongside broader questions about gender and social respectability.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: discuss the difference between advice and command. 10–22: classify practical instructions and warnings. 22–35: analyse the two interruptions. 35–45: discuss care and control together. 45–50: exit ticket on the ending’s effect.

## Questions
How does punctuation shape pace? What does the daughter’s limited opportunity to speak reveal? Why does the bread question become a judgement about reputation?

# Raja Rao · The Cow of the Barricades
Functional English II · Semester 3

## Story overview
A mysterious cow, Gauri, visits the Master regularly on Tuesdays. She accepts the grain he offers and then disappears. People search for her without finding a clear owner or ordinary explanation. Her unusual behaviour and her connection with the Master encourage villagers to treat her with reverence. The story also refers to her contact with Mahatma Gandhi; the Master and Gandhi should not simply be assumed to be the same character.

As political tensions increase, barricades divide the town, with armed authorities on one side and people resisting on the other. Gauri walks through the gathering. The crowd honours her and helps her onto the barricade. The chief of the opposing soldiers shoots her, and she dies. The narrative presents the absence of visible blood and the crowd’s reactions in a legendary, devotional register.

Afterwards a patron erects a statue of Gauri. Children play around it and toy Gauris circulate. The Master imagines her waiting to be reborn when India again suffers before freedom. The ending connects remembrance, popular legend and the freedom struggle, without describing Gauri as a literal historical participant in a documented event.

## Interpretation
The cow can represent compassion, nonviolence or collective hopes, but the story’s religious and political symbols invite debate rather than one compulsory equation. The narrative mixes colloquial storytelling, mythic imagery and political conflict. Ask how the community makes meaning from her death and whether the ending is wholly consoling.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: identify narrator and setting. 10–22: trace Gauri’s visits. 22–35: reconstruct the barricade scene. 35–45: discuss statue, myth and political memory. 45–50: exit ticket on a detail that supports an interpretation.

## Questions
How does the story establish Gauri’s mystery? What changes when she reaches the barricades? How does the ending join play, remembrance and hope?

# Aldous Huxley · The Beauty Industry
Functional English II · Semester 3

## Argument overview
Huxley’s satirical essay considers the growth of the beauty industry and the money and attention devoted to appearance. He discusses changing social conditions and the increased availability and use of beauty products, then questions whether external treatment alone can produce the kind of beauty he values. He contrasts physical presentation with qualities of mind, feeling or character. His statistics and comparisons belong to the historical context of the essay and should be checked in the assigned text rather than repeated as current figures.

## Method and interpretation
The essay uses irony, exaggeration and contrasts to criticise consumer culture and narrow ideas of appearance. At the same time, a critical reader can question Huxley’s assumptions: his discussion often singles out women, risks judging people’s inner lives from their looks and treats some beauty practices as superficial without considering autonomy, work, pleasure or social pressure. Explain his argument fairly before evaluating its limits. Appearance does not reliably reveal moral character.

## Teaching plan: 50 minutes
0–10: distinguish an author’s claim from agreement with it. 10–22: map Huxley’s evidence and central contrast. 22–35: identify a satirical technique. 35–45: evaluate gender assumptions and present-day relevance. 45–50: write a claim with one support and one limitation.

## Questions
How does satire shape the reader’s response? What social conditions does Huxley connect with beauty products? Which assumptions in the essay can be challenged, and why?

# Seamus Heaney · Digging
Functional English II · Semester 3

## Poem summary
At a desk the speaker holds a pen. He hears a spade outside and looks down at his father digging. The sight carries him back to his father’s earlier work digging potatoes, remembered through skilled movements and the cool feel of the crop. He also remembers his grandfather cutting turf in a bog and recalls bringing him milk before the older man returned to work.

The smell of earth and sound of cutting make these memories vivid. The speaker recognises that he does not follow the earlier generations with a spade. Returning to the pen in his hand, he decides to dig with it: writing will be his own form of careful work and exploration.

## Form and interpretation
The poem moves from present observation to memories and back to the pen. The opening compares the pen to a gun; the ending emphasises a different tool and action. Do not insist that the gun image has only one political or personal meaning. Sound patterns, tactile detail and the repeated action of digging honour manual skill while allowing a different vocation. The poem negotiates continuity and difference rather than simply rejecting family work.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: sketch the three generations. 10–22: follow the shifts in time. 22–35: identify sound and sensory details. 35–45: compare pen and spade. 45–50: explain one effect using a precise detail.

## Questions
What triggers memory? How are the father’s and grandfather’s work represented? Why is the final act of digging figurative?

course-19:2.text:
# Amitav Ghosh · The Town by the Sea
Functional English II · Semester 3

## Context and limitation
The assigned essay relates to the 26 December 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami and its consequences in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Anthologies may abridge the longer account. This note provides a broad, source-based outline; check the prescribed extract for exact names, sequence and detail. The subject involves bereavement and disaster and should be discussed sensitively.

## Outline
Ghosh’s account considers a town on Car Nicobar after the tsunami and the experience of a researcher whose family and home were caught in the disaster. The man is away when the earthquake and waves strike. His son survives, while his wife and daughter are lost. The narrator’s conversations and the damaged landscape connect a large-scale catastrophe with a particular family’s grief.

The account’s attention to surviving structures, everyday belongings and memories shows how material places can carry personal meaning. It also raises difficult questions about how people speak, remember and continue after loss. A reader should not judge a person’s grief from one gesture or conclude that valuing work or possessions proves a lack of love.

## Reading critically
Distinguish the narrator’s observations, another person’s recollections and your own inferences. The tsunami was a physical disaster with social consequences; describing nature’s power should not erase differences in vulnerability, aid or human responsibility. Use respectful language and avoid presenting tragedy as a simple moral lesson.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: context and content note. 10–22: identify narrator, place and event. 22–35: trace one remembered object or place in the extract. 35–45: discuss the limits of inferring emotion. 45–50: write a question for the text rather than a judgement of the survivor.

## Questions
How does a specific family story affect our understanding of a disaster? What can objects reveal, and what can they not prove?

Read the assigned text and verify its wording and selection against the course anthology.

course-19:2.title: Sujata Bhatt · A Different History
course-19:2.text:
# Sujata Bhatt · A Different History
Functional English II · Semester 3

## Poem summary
The opening imagines the Greek god Pan migrating to India. Gods appear in forms associated with the natural world, and trees and books are treated with reverence. The speaker lists ways of handling a book carelessly and asks that pages be turned gently, respecting Sarasvati, associated with knowledge, and the tree from which the paper came.

The poem then turns to questions about language and oppression. Images of violent conquest complicate the earlier reverence for books and learning. The speaker asks how later generations can come to love a language connected with an oppressor’s history. The ending is a question and a paradox, not a declaration that the violence has been forgotten or that the language has only one meaning.

## Form and interpretation
Allusions to Pan and Sarasvati bring different traditions into relation. The shift from respectful instruction to questioning and violent imagery creates tension between language as knowledge and language implicated in power. A language is not literally a person who decides to kill: examine how the rhetorical questions make readers consider its historical uses. Readers can debate the emotional force of the final “love” without claiming that pain is necessarily absent.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: identify the two movements. 10–22: discuss books, trees and deities. 22–35: examine the shift to questions about language. 35–45: discuss inheritance and colonial history. 45–50: exit response explaining one contrast.

## Questions
Why connect a book to a tree? How does the tone change? What makes the later generation’s relationship to language complex?

# R. K. Narayan · Engine Trouble
Functional English II · Semester 3

## Story from beginning to end
The narrator wins a road engine in a lottery at a travelling fair called Gaiety Land. What initially looks like a valuable prize immediately becomes a problem: it is large, heavy and difficult to move or sell. The fair’s management allows it to remain temporarily, but after the fair leaves the municipality demands that the narrator remove it or pay rent for the space.

Unable to find a buyer, he pays rent and spends increasing amounts trying to deal with the machine. When the ground is needed for another event, he arranges to move it to a friend’s property. He hires a temple elephant, labourers and Joseph, a former bus driver, to help direct the engine. Their efforts are not coordinated. The machine damages a compound wall, the elephant becomes agitated, and the owner and authorities hold the narrator responsible. What was supposed to be a windfall has become a source of debt, public embarrassment and domestic tension.

A visiting swami announces a performance involving a road engine driven over his body. The narrator hopes that allowing his engine to be used will finally solve his transport problem. The dangerous demonstration is stopped by the authorities, so this plan fails too. He considers leaving town.

An earthquake then shifts the engine into a disused well. The narrator fears another liability, but the well’s owner had been ordered to close it and welcomes the machine because it effectively fills the opening. The owner agrees to settle the problem and cover expenses in return for leaving the engine there. An accident finally resolves what careful efforts could not. The narrator is relieved.

## Technique and themes
First-person narration, escalating complications and reversals make the story comic. The prize’s supposed value depends on the owner’s ability to store, move or use it. Coincidence and absurdity shape the resolution; the story does not require readers to believe that disasters are generally fortunate. Consider the narrator’s perspective and the other people affected by his schemes.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: discuss whether every prize is useful. 10–25: make a cause-and-effect chain from lottery to failed moves. 25–35: analyse the swami episode and earthquake. 35–45: discuss irony and practical value. 45–50: exit ticket explaining the final reversal.

## Questions
Why is the engine a burden? How does each attempted solution create another problem? Why does the well owner welcome it?

Read the assigned text and verify its wording and selection against the course anthology.

course-19:3.text:
# Erich Fromm · Is Love an Art?
Functional English II · Semester 3

## Context and central question
“Is Love an Art?” is associated with the opening of Fromm’s The Art of Loving (1956). The exact course extract should be checked. Fromm asks whether love is a skill requiring knowledge and effort or a pleasant feeling that happens by chance. He argues for the former.

## Main line of argument
Fromm suggests that many people focus on being loved—becoming attractive, successful or desirable—rather than developing their own capacity to love. A second assumption treats love mainly as a problem of finding the right object, rather than practising an ability. A third confuses the initial experience of falling in love with the continuing work of loving. These are Fromm’s diagnoses of cultural attitudes, not universal facts about every relationship.

If love is an art, he argues, a person must give it serious attention, learn both theory and practice, and recognise that improvement takes effort. In the broader book he links mature love with care, responsibility, respect and knowledge; check whether those later discussions occur within the assigned extract before attributing them to the opening alone.

## Evaluate the argument
Fromm’s framework invites reflection on attention, reciprocity and whether consumer habits shape relationships. Ask whether the analogy with an art has limits: relationships also depend on other people’s agency, social conditions, consent and circumstances beyond one person’s control. Effort does not obligate anyone to remain in an unsafe or unwanted relationship.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: distinguish falling in love from sustaining care. 10–22: map the three assumptions Fromm questions. 22–35: assess his art analogy. 35–45: offer an example and a counterexample. 45–50: write one reasoned agreement or disagreement.

## Questions
What does it mean to treat love as a capacity? Why does Fromm distinguish being loved from loving? What are the limits of the skill analogy?

Read the assigned text and verify its wording and selection against the course anthology.

# Communication, greetings, requests and telephone skills
Functional English II · Semester 3

## Understanding communication
Communication involves producing, receiving and interpreting messages in a context. A sender’s intention is not automatically the same as the listener’s understanding. Feedback—questions, paraphrases and responses—helps identify misunderstandings. Noise can include poor audio, ambiguous wording, interruptions or different assumptions.

## Greetings and introductions
Choose an appropriate greeting for the relationship and situation. In a formal introduction, give your name and relevant role: “Good morning. I’m Meena, a student in the English department.” In an informal setting, a shorter greeting may be appropriate. Pronounce and use another person’s name respectfully; do not assume a person’s preferred title.

## Making requests
A useful request states the action, context and, when appropriate, a realistic deadline. “Could you please share the meeting notes by Friday?” is more specific than “Send it soon.” Choose a tone suited to the situation, and allow the other person to ask questions or decline. Politeness is not the same as excessive length.

## Telephone communication
Before calling, identify your purpose and necessary information. Greet the person, introduce yourself and check whether it is a convenient time. Explain the reason for calling, listen, confirm important names or dates and summarise any agreed next steps. If the line is unclear, ask for repetition rather than pretending to understand. Avoid sharing private information without confirming identity and authorisation.

## Model call
“Good morning. This is Meena from the English department. May I speak to the library coordinator?” If the person is unavailable: “Could you please ask them to call me back? My number is …” Repeat the number slowly and thank the recipient. This is a model, not a real contact.

## 50-minute lesson
0–10: identify the parts of a communication exchange. 10–20: practise formal and informal greetings. 20–30: rewrite vague requests. 30–42: pairs role-play a call and take a message. 42–50: confirm details and reflect on one listening skill.

## Questions
How can you politely check whether someone is available? What information belongs in a telephone message? Why is feedback important?
